metadata.title: Indigenous and non-Indigenous proficiency gaps for out-of-school and in-school populations: A machine learning approach

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses OECD PISA for Development 2017 (PISA-D) microdata for two populations: an in-school sample of 15-year-olds in grade 7 and an out-of-school youth (OOSY) household-based sample aged 14–16. The analytic samples are restricted to three countries (Guatemala, Paraguay, Senegal) after excluding Panama and Honduras from the respective subsamples. The paper does not report the use of PISA-D sampling/survey weights or replicate-weight procedures in the ML treatment-effect estimation; instead it focuses on lasso-based control selection and AIPW/DML estimation with logit models. Because the manuscript does not document weight variables (e.g., TOTWGT/W_FSTUWT) or replicate design methods, the weighting approach for complex survey design cannot be confirmed from the provided text.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are binary achievement thresholds (reaching at least specific PISA-D proficiency levels in math and reading), not PV-based continuous achievement scores. As a result, plausible values are not the direct target of the analysis, and PV handling is not applicable to the reported ML treatment-effect setup. The manuscript also does not describe how missing covariate data were handled (e.g., complete-case deletion vs imputation), which is a reporting gap because missingness can affect high-dimensional lasso selection and treatment-effect estimation.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Uses PISA-D 2017 two datasets: (1) in-school sample of students attending school at grade 7 (15-year-olds) including seven countries, then excludes Panama (not in the in-school sample) and Honduras (low Indigenous rate) to form the working set of Guatemala, Paraguay, and Senegal; (2) out-of-school sample (OOSY) of youth aged 14–16 from a household-based survey in five countries, then excludes countries not in the working set to retain Guatemala, Paraguay, and Senegal. Indigenous status is defined by language spoken at home (test language vs Indigenous languages: Maya in Guatemala, Guarani in Paraguay, and French vs Pular/Serer/Diola/Wolof in Senegal). Outcomes are binary indicators for reaching at least specified PISA-D proficiency levels in math and reading (with level 2 for math/reading not estimated for the out-of-school sample due to near-zero rates).

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA-D 2017 Out-of-school youth (OOSY) age 14–16, Math proficiency levels
main_findings.target_variable: Math achievement (binary: reach at least level 1c/1b/1a)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Best-performing specification (Cross validation, Panel C, Table 4): ATET coefficients for Indigenous vs non-Indigenous are -0.1297 (level 1c, p<0.01) and -0.0872 (level 1b, p<0.01); level 1a is -0.0149 (not significant).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA-D 2017 out-of-school youth the study leveraged SES index, mother literacy, rural location, school safety, and work (care) to predict binary math proficiency thresholds, finding that Indigenous youth had 12.97% fewer chances to reach level 1c and 8.72% fewer chances to reach level 1b than non-Indigenous youth (with no significant gap at level 1a). This indicates that out-of-school Indigenous learners face persistent disadvantages concentrated at the lower-to-intermediate end of the math distribution, suggesting that dropout-prevention and early numeracy support for Indigenous youth should be prioritized before they disengage from schooling, though causality cannot be fully established from the reported ML-based treatment-effect framework and survey-weight handling is not documented.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA-D 2017 Out-of-school youth (OOSY) age 14–16, Reading proficiency levels
main_findings.target_variable: Reading achievement (binary: reach at least level 1c/1b/1a)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Best-performing specification (Adaptive lasso, Panel D, Table 5): ATET coefficients for Indigenous vs non-Indigenous are -0.0228 (level 1c, p<0.01), -0.1960 (level 1b, p<0.01), and -0.0386 (level 1a, p<0.01).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA-D 2017 out-of-school youth the study leveraged SES index, number of books, mother literacy, travel time, and school books/notebooks to predict binary reading proficiency thresholds, finding that Indigenous youth had significantly lower chances across all three reading levels, with the largest gap at level 1b (about -19.6%). This indicates that language-linked exclusion and associated household disadvantages strongly affect reading attainment even before students are in school, suggesting that targeted language-support and learning-material interventions for out-of-school Indigenous youth could substantially reduce reading gaps, while the study’s reliance on ML-based treatment-effect estimation and unreported missing-data handling limits certainty about causal magnitude.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA-D 2017 In-school sample (grade 7, age 15), Math proficiency levels
main_findings.target_variable: Math achievement (binary: reach at least level 1c/1b/1a/level 2)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Best-performing specification (Cross validation, Panel C, Table 4): ATET coefficients for Indigenous vs non-Indigenous are -0.0896 (level 1b, p<0.05) and -0.0693 (level 1a, p<0.05); level 1c is 0.0045 (not significant) and level 2 is -0.0162 (not significant).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA-D 2017 in-school grade 7 the study leveraged infrastructure, student-teacher ratio, teacher qualification, SES, and disability to predict binary math proficiency thresholds, finding that Indigenous students had lower chances of reaching the middle and upper-middle of the math distribution (about -8.96% at level 1b and -6.93% at level 1a) relative to non-Indigenous students. This indicates that even within school, Indigenous disadvantage persists in math attainment for students who are not at the very bottom or top, implying that in-school instructional and resource equity measures should target Indigenous students’ progression through the middle of the achievement distribution, though the paper reports no explicit survey-weight strategy and missing-data handling is not documented.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA-D 2017 In-school sample (grade 7, age 15), Reading proficiency levels
main_findings.target_variable: Reading achievement (binary: reach at least level 1c/1b/1a/level 2)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Best-performing specification (Cross validation, Panel C, Table 5): ATET coefficients for Indigenous vs non-Indigenous are -0.0069 (level 1b, not significant), -0.0568 (level 1a, p<0.05), and -0.0556 (level 2, p<0.01); level 1c is -0.0051 (not significant).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA-D 2017 in-school grade 7 the study leveraged infrastructure, teacher professional development, number of books, mother literacy, and safety to predict binary reading proficiency thresholds, finding that Indigenous students had significantly lower chances of reaching higher reading levels (about -5.68% at level 1a and -5.56% at level 2) compared with non-Indigenous students. This indicates that reading gaps for Indigenous students are most pronounced at the upper end of the in-school reading distribution, suggesting that policies should focus on strengthening instructional quality and language-relevant supports for Indigenous students’ advancement, while the ML-based treatment-effect approach and unreported missing-data strategy constrain interpretation of effect sizes.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses OECD PISA for Development 2017 (PISA-D) microdata to estimate Indigenous vs non-Indigenous learning gaps in three countries (Guatemala, Paraguay, Senegal) using two subsamples: out-of-school youth aged 14–16 and in-school students in grade 7 (age 15). Outcomes are binary indicators for reaching at least specific PISA-D proficiency levels in math and reading (e.g., level 1c/1b/1a and level 2 where applicable), and the treatment is Indigenous status defined by language spoken at home. The main ML-based treatment-effect approach combines lasso control selection with augmented inverse probability weighting (AIPW) and robustness via double machine learning (DML) with cross-fitting. Reported ATET coefficients show negative gaps for Indigenous youth across multiple math/reading thresholds, with the largest out-of-school reading gap at level 1b (≈ −0.20) and significant in-school reading gaps at higher levels (≈ −0.056 to −0.055). Limitations include lack of documented survey-weight usage and missing-data handling, and the fact that ML-based feature selection does not by itself establish causal effects.
